items.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017
items.q: I’ll tell you who has probably very good insight, and you should talk to him if you haven’t already, is Loren Schoenberg at the Jazz Museum in Harlem.

ctx.x: I bet today there would be a designated psychological definition for what he was about. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Yeah. I’ll tell you who has probably very good insight, and you should talk to him if you haven’t already, is Loren Schoenberg at the Jazz Museum in Harlem. Because he worked with Benny for a number of years. And he got the full treatment, everything from praise to damnation, he got the whole thing. And Benny took his band away from him eventually. He took off his gloves man.
Touché. You know Joe Wilder, he went on that tour to Russia.

items.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019
items.q: I wound up kind of becoming a fill in radio announcer at WGBO because there was a show called “Jazz from the Archives” with Dan Morgenstern and Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote. And I was kind of like an adopted son or something. So I started doing these shows with them.

ctx.x: We’ve been at this for quite a while, so we’re going to have to do Part Two, but I wanted to ask you about the Jazz Museum in Harlem. Did you have to interview for that position, and did you give them a philosophy, a pitch so to speak?

In the early 1990s I started to branch out a little bit more. I was involved with something called the American Jazz Orchestra, with John Lewis, that started in 1985, 1986. And this was a band comprised of mostly big band veterans: Marvin Stamm, Virgil Jones, John Eckert, Benny Powell, Jimmy Knepper, Eddie Bert, I think I said him, Danny Bank and Jerry Dodgion and Jerome Richardson and Bill Easley and Dick Katz and great bass players including we made a record with Ron Carter and Howard Collins on guitar. It was…

would conduct when John wasn’t there. Then Mel Lewis had been working for years with what they call the Westdeutscher Rundfunk, which is the radio orchestra in Cologne Germany. And he got me on that. So for two summers I conducted that orchestra in Cologne. Did the “Rhapsody in Blue” and there’s a funny story about that with Gunther Schuller. And the “Rhapsody in Blue” and the Paul Whiteman program with the full arrangements for the strings and all this kind of stuff. And did another concert with Milt Grayson who…
